body:
Identifying ritual activity

A ritual is an action performed according to an established custom, often with religious or symbolic significance.

Ritual practices may involve bathing, offerings, fire, symbolic objects or gatherings at particular places.

Harappan settlements contain several structures that have been interpreted as ritual installations. However, the precise purposes of these structures are not always known.

Unlike ordinary domestic facilities, some structures were unusually elaborate or situated in distinctive public areas. Their construction and location have encouraged interpretations involving ceremonial activity.

The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro

The Great Bath is one of the best-known structures of the Harappan civilisation.

It was located in the elevated Citadel area of Mohenjodaro.

The structure consisted of a large rectangular tank surrounded by a courtyard and associated rooms. Steps provided access to the tank from 2 sides.

The tank was carefully constructed with bricks and waterproofing arrangements. Water could be supplied and subsequently drained away.

Was the Great Bath a religious structure?

Its unusual construction, controlled water arrangements and location within the Citadel suggest that it may have been intended for a special activity.

One important interpretation is that the Great Bath was used for ritual bathing.

However, this remains an interpretation rather than an established fact.

The Harappans also possessed ordinary domestic bathing areas. Therefore, the existence of the Great Bath does not mean that all bathing was religious.

Nor does the structure establish the identity of a particular deity, priesthood or organised religious institution.

The Great Bath is certainly a major water structure at Mohenjodaro. Its use for special or ritual bathing is plausible, but its exact purpose is not conclusively known.

Fire altars and ritual installations

Structures interpreted as fire altars have been discovered at several Harappan sites.

Two especially important locations are:

  • Kalibangan in Rajasthan: Structures interpreted as fire altars have been found in association with domestic and other areas, including installations in the Citadel.
  • Lothal in Gujarat: Excavations revealed installations interpreted as fire altars in residential and other parts of the settlement.

Some installations contained evidence of burning, including ash and charcoal. Their forms and contexts have led excavators to associate them with possible ritual activity.

However, the exact ceremonies performed at these installations remain uncertain.

Fire altars and Vedic rituals

Fire played an important role in later Vedic sacrificial practices. This resemblance has encouraged comparisons between Harappan fire installations and later fire rituals.

Such comparisons must be treated carefully.

The identification of a structure as a fire altar does not automatically establish the performance of a Vedic yajna, the worship of a particular fire deity or the existence of a Vedic priestly institution.

Evidence of burning can help identify how a structure was used, but it does not by itself reveal the prayers, beliefs or complete ceremony associated with that activity.

Public and ceremonial spaces in Gujarat

Dholavira contained a substantial open area associated with its planned urban layout. This has been described as a ceremonial ground and may have accommodated public gatherings or other collective activities.

Such a space demonstrates that some areas of the settlement may have been intended for activities extending beyond ordinary household life.

Its precise use, however, is not fully established. A public gathering space does not necessarily represent a temple or a religious sanctuary.

Were there Harappan temples?

No large structure has been securely identified as a temple equivalent to the well-established temples known from later Indian historical periods.

This does not prove that the Harappans had no religious buildings or organised worship. It means that the available remains do not permit confident identification of such institutions.

The distinction between the absence of confirmed evidence and proof of absence is important.

What religious conclusions are reasonable?

Harappan figurines, symbolic seals and unusual structures suggest that ritual and symbolic activities formed part of the civilisation's cultural life.

Nevertheless, the surviving evidence does not establish a single uniform religion followed by all Harappan communities.

Regional differences in settlements and artefacts also make it possible that religious customs varied between places.

The best-supported conclusion is that the Harappans possessed symbolic practices and possibly specialised ritual activities, while the identity of their deities and the organisation of their religious institutions remain uncertain.

Prelims focus

  • The Great Bath was located at Mohenjodaro.
  • The Great Bath has been interpreted as a possible ritual-bathing structure.
  • Structures identified as fire altars have been found at Kalibangan in Rajasthan.
  • Fire-altars have also been reported from Lothal in Gujarat.
  • Dholavira possessed a large open area interpreted as a possible ceremonial ground.
  • No unmistakable large temple has been securely identified in the Harappan archaeological record.
  • Trap: Harappan fire altars are not conclusive evidence of later Vedic sacrificial practices.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, Section 3.3, The Citadel, p. 8, and Section 11.2, Problems of Interpretation, pp. 23–24; Archaeological Survey of India, Excavations at Kalibangan: The Harappans, Introduction and a Summary of the Results, discussion of fire-altars; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, pp. 91–93; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Possible Places and Practices of Ritual

body:
The treatment of the dead

Burial practices provide important evidence about how a community treated its dead.

At many Harappan sites, the dead were placed in pits dug into the ground. The body was generally laid out in an extended position, although practices and details varied between sites.

The surviving graves reveal some funerary customs, but do not provide a complete account of Harappan religious beliefs.

Construction of burial pits

Harappan graves were not all constructed in exactly the same manner.

Some consisted of relatively simple earth pits, while others included brick-lined spaces or additional arrangements.

These differences may have reflected local customs, available resources or the social position of the deceased.

However, the variations do not establish a fixed hierarchy of burial classes.

Objects placed with the dead

Some Harappan graves contained pottery, ornaments or other objects.

Among the recorded finds were:

  • Pottery vessels placed near the deceased.
  • Beads and other personal ornaments.
  • Jewellery associated with both male and female burials.
  • Copper mirrors in some graves.

Such objects may have been personal possessions, funerary offerings or items associated with beliefs about death.

Their presence has sometimes been interpreted as suggesting a belief that objects might be useful after death.

However, this interpretation cannot be confirmed solely from the objects themselves.

Did Harappan burials reflect great inequalities?

Harappan graves generally contain comparatively modest quantities of valuable goods.

Unlike the elaborate royal tombs of ancient Egypt, the known Harappan burial record does not reveal a comparable tradition of enormous royal graves filled with wealth.

This distinction is important because the Harappans possessed valuable objects during life, yet these were not commonly deposited in large quantities with the dead.

The limited presence of valuable grave goods does not prove complete equality. It indicates that burial wealth is not a strong or straightforward measure of Harappan social rank.

A society may possess economic inequalities without expressing them through elaborate graves. Therefore, relatively modest Harappan burials do not establish that every Harappan enjoyed the same wealth or social position.

Burial practices at Harappa

The cemetery known as R-37 at Harappa provides important evidence of extended inhumation, meaning burial of the uncremated body laid out at full length.

Graves could contain pottery and personal ornaments, while their construction sometimes differed.

These findings establish the practice of burial but do not conclusively identify the social position or religious beliefs of the individuals buried there.

Gujarat connection: Joint burials at Lothal

Lothal provides an important example of regional variation in Harappan burial customs.

Excavations revealed graves containing the remains of 2 individuals in the same burial pit. Such graves are commonly described as joint burials.

The excavation report documented 3 regular joint burials at Lothal.

The presence of 2 bodies in a grave demonstrates a shared burial arrangement. It does not establish that the individuals were husband and wife, nor does it reveal the circumstances of their deaths.

Attempts to connect such burials directly with later practices such as sati are unsupported by secure evidence.

Therefore, the important established fact is the occurrence of joint burials at Lothal, not a particular explanation of the relationship between the deceased.

Gujarat connection: Memorial burials at Dholavira

Dholavira, in the Rann of Kutch, possessed an extensive cemetery located to the west of the fortified city.

An unusual feature of this cemetery is the presence of cenotaphs.

Cenotaph

A cenotaph is a memorial structure associated with a deceased person or persons that does not contain their bodily remains.

Many of Dholavira's funerary structures are interpreted as memorials rather than ordinary graves containing human bodies.

These structures demonstrate that the Harappans did not necessarily use a single burial or memorial practice throughout their civilisation.

The exact beliefs associated with Dholavira's cenotaphs remain uncertain.

Distinguishing major burial forms

The differences between these forms are straightforward:

  • Individual pit burial: A burial pit containing the remains of an individual.
  • Joint burial: A grave containing the remains of 2 or more individuals.
  • Cenotaph: A memorial associated with the dead that does not contain the bodily remains of the person or persons commemorated.

These categories describe the physical character of the burial or memorial. They do not automatically explain the religious ceremony or social relationship involved.

What do burial practices establish about Harappan religion?

Harappan burial customs indicate that some communities followed recognised practices for treating the dead. The occasional placement of objects with bodies may suggest symbolic or religious beliefs concerning death.

However, the burial record does not establish a detailed doctrine of the afterlife, a single uniform funeral ceremony or a named religious tradition followed throughout the civilisation.

Nor can the presence of ornaments, pottery or mirrors reliably establish a person's caste, religious office or political rank.

Connecting society, authority, religion and burial

The evidence for Harappan society becomes clearer when its major features are considered together.

Residential buildings reveal organised household life. Differences in valuable objects and housing suggest economic and social differentiation. Standardised construction and planned settlements indicate coordinated decisions, although the precise political authority is unknown.

Figurines, seals and unusual structures suggest symbolic and possibly religious activities, but their exact meanings remain disputed. Burial customs demonstrate different ways of treating and remembering the dead without establishing a complete religious system.

The general principle is that physical evidence establishes the existence of objects and practices more securely than it establishes their complete social, political or religious meanings.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan bodies were commonly placed in burial pits.
  • Some graves contained pottery, ornaments or copper mirrors.
  • Jewellery has been found in both male and female burials.
  • Harappa's R-37 cemetery provides evidence of extended burials.
  • Lothal in Gujarat is associated with joint burials.
  • Dholavira in Gujarat contains unusual memorial funerary structures, including cenotaphs.
  • Trap: Joint burial does not prove a husband-wife relationship or the practice of sati.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, Section 4.1, Burials, p. 9, and Section 11.2, Problems of Interpretation, pp. 23–24; Archaeological Survey of India, S. R. Rao, Lothal: A Harappan Port Town (1955–62), Volume I, 1979, Chapter VIII, The Cemetery, pp. 137 and 140–141; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis and Statement of Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 17 November 2026.]
